Silesia Alert, unlike most applications that use generally available weather radars, has its own ultra-modern and extremely precise warning generator. So far it has been used for scientific purposes and now it has been made available for our application. Radar located at the Goczałkowice Reservoir in the Silesian Voivodeship. Its range is a radius of 200 km, thanks to which it covers the entire Silesian Voivodeship, part of Lesser Poland and the province of Opole, as well as a large part of the Tatras and Beskids.

How does the Silesia Alert app work?
Our application is an innovative tool that analyzes radar data in real time, checking whether there are storms within the radar range and whether there is a risk of extreme phenomena such as hail, strong wind, whirlwinds or torrential rainfall. The application therefore replaces the user in the independent viewing and interpretation of radar data.

Weather warnings and alerts
An innovative algorithm that detects the risk of dangerous phenomena operates in 39 largest cities within the radar range, i.e. within a radius of 200 km from Goczałkowice-Zdrój, where our radar operates. If a storm occurs within a radius of 15 km from a given city from a list of 39 cities, which meets the criteria of specialized radar parameters, talking about possible threats, a threat warning is issued. In this case, the application sends a notification immediately after issuing such an alert.
There are 6 degrees of danger. No threats mean no notifications and the green color of the icon in the application next to a given city. If a strong storm is detected, alerts are displayed with grades ranging from "1" (lowest) to "5" (highest). "5" represents the greatest threat and the course of the storm can be very violent. Receiving a warning means that within a radius of 15 km from the geographical center of the selected city, there is a strong storm at the moment, which may also pose a threat to us in the next few minutes, thanks to which we have a few or a dozen (sometimes more) minutes to react.
